opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the starting point for me is to look at how people, and scientists in particular, actually come to understand the world. We almost never jump straight to the right theory in one shot. What we do is start with some rough, partial model, maybe just a few pieces we're fairly confident about, and then we probe it. We run an experiment, we notice where the predictions break, and we go back and revise a specific part of the model rather than throwing the whole thing out. That incremental, piece-by-piece process is, I think, the core of how intelligence handles genuinely novel situations.

The "compositional" part matters because the world itself is compositional. It's made of objects, mechanisms, and causal relationships that recombine in endless ways. If your hypotheses are built out of reusable components, little programs or causal mechanisms, then when you encounter something new you don't have to learn it from scratch. You can say, "This looks like gravity plus some friction plus an agent pushing on things," and you assemble a candidate explanation from parts you already understand. That gives you enormous sample efficiency, which is exactly what current deep learning systems struggle with. They tend to need huge amounts of data because they're essentially learning a monolithic function rather than a structured model.

The "refinement" part matters because the space of possible hypotheses is astronomically large. You can't enumerate it, and you can't just sample blindly. But if you have a current hypothesis and a specific piece of evidence that contradicts it, that tells you a lot about *where* to look. You can localize the error to one component and edit that, the way a programmer debugs code. So search becomes tractable: instead of searching over all possible theories, you're searching over small edits to a theory that's already mostly right.

There's also an interpretability and trust angle. A hypothesis that's built compositionally is something you can inspect. You can ask, "Which assumption is doing the work here?" and test that assumption directly. That's very different from a black-box model where you can't really tell why it believes what it believes.

And finally, I think it connects to active learning and experimentation. If an AI system holds explicit, structured hypotheses, it can reason about which experiment would best distinguish between them. That closes the loop: hypothesize, design a test, observe, refine. To me, that loop, done compositionally, is much closer to what we mean by understanding than just fitting patterns in a static dataset. It's how you get systems that can actually do science, not just summarize it.

r001.rationale: The response says people, especially scientists, begin with rough partial models, test them, and revise specific parts when predictions fail.

r002.rationale: It identifies the enormous hypothesis space as a search challenge and explains that contradictory evidence can guide search toward localized edits to a current hypothesis.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core of it is that the world has structure, and that structure is compositional. If you look at how we actually come to understand anything, whether it's a physicist building a model of a system or a child figuring out how a toy works, you don't arrive at the right hypothesis in one shot. You start with something coarse, something that's probably wrong in a lot of ways, and then you refine it. You notice where it fails, you add a piece, you swap out a component, you specialize a general rule to a particular case. The hypothesis at the end is built out of parts, and those parts were themselves built out of parts.

So when I say compositional refinement, I mean two things at once. Compositional means your hypotheses are made of reusable pieces that fit together in principled ways, like functions in a programming language. And refinement means you move through the space of hypotheses incrementally, where each step is a small modification of what you already had, rather than sampling something entirely new from scratch.

The reason I think this matters for AI is largely about search. The space of possible explanations for any interesting phenomenon is astronomically large. If you treat that space as flat, where every hypothesis is just a point and you're trying to find the good ones, you're hopeless. But if the space has compositional structure, then a hypothesis that's partially right is informative about its neighbors. Knowing that one component is working lets you keep it fixed and focus your effort on the parts that aren't. That's an enormous reduction in what you have to explore.

There's also an epistemic argument, which is that compositional hypotheses are interpretable and transferable in a way that monolithic ones aren't. If I learn a piece of a model in one context, say a notion of containment or collision, I can carry that piece into a different problem. Humans do this constantly. We don't relearn gravity every time we see a new object fall. We have a component and we reuse it. A system that develops its hypotheses by composition inherits that property almost for free.

And I'd contrast this with what a lot of current deep learning does, which is essentially fit one giant parametric function to data. That works remarkably well for prediction, but the resulting model isn't a hypothesis in the scientific sense. You can't point to the part of it that encodes some claim about the world and ask whether that claim is true, or revise just that claim when it turns out to be wrong. Refinement is only really possible when there are discrete parts to refine.

So the short version is: the world is built from parts, our knowledge of it should be built from parts, and the way to get there is to let the system propose structured hypotheses and iteratively improve them in response to evidence, the way science itself works.

r001.rationale: It says people develop understanding by starting with coarse hypotheses and refining them as they notice failures, add pieces, or specialize rules.

r002.rationale: It identifies the enormous hypothesis search space as a challenge and explains that partially correct hypotheses can guide refinement by preserving working components and focusing effort on what fails.

astra-6.text:
Well, a hypothesis usually has structure. It’s made up of smaller claims about how the world works, and those claims can be combined or revised. If I think an object moved because something pushed it, I can refine that explanation by asking what pushed it, under what conditions, and whether another force was involved. I don’t have to discard the entire explanation every time I encounter new evidence.

That’s useful for learning because it lets you reuse what you already understand. You can take familiar components and compose them into an explanation of a situation you’ve never seen before. And it gives you a way to investigate mistakes: which part of the hypothesis failed, and what observation or experiment would help distinguish possible replacements?

Of course, composition alone doesn’t make a hypothesis correct. You still have to test it against the world. The attraction is that refinement makes that process more systematic: propose an explanation, examine its consequences, and change the parts that the evidence gives you reason to change.

r001.rationale: The speaker describes refining an explanation by revising smaller claims while preserving the rest, and frames this as a reasoning process a person can use.

r002.rationale: The response discusses investigating mistakes and testing explanations, but does not identify guiding or reinforcing productive refinement paths as a challenge in mechanizing hypothesis development.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the world has structure, and we want our hypotheses to reflect that structure. If you’re trying to understand a complicated phenomenon, you usually don’t invent a complete explanation in one step. You start with something simple, see where it fails, and then refine it. Perhaps you introduce another variable, change a relationship, or break one mechanism into several interacting mechanisms.

Compositionality makes that process useful because the pieces can be reused. You can preserve the parts of an explanation that work while changing the part that doesn’t. And those same pieces can appear in explanations of other phenomena. So learning becomes a process of building on what you already understand.

But the crucial thing is that refinement has to be constrained by evidence. Making a hypothesis more elaborate isn’t necessarily progress. You want to ask: does this change explain something we couldn’t explain before? Does it make a prediction we can test? Ideally, the system develops hypotheses that are both increasingly expressive and still open to criticism and revision.

r001.rationale: It says people develop explanations by starting simple, seeing where they fail, and refining them, presenting this as a useful model for AI hypothesis development.

r002.rationale: It says refinement should be constrained by evidence and testable predictions, but does not identify guiding or reinforcing productive paths as a challenge in mechanizing hypothesis development.
